problem: Triangular billiards – does every triangle have a periodic billiards path?
missing_details: Definition of a billiard trajectory as the motion of a point particle in straight lines inside the triangle with specular reflections (angle of incidence equals angle of reflection)
Specification that a trajectory terminates if it reaches a vertex (extinction at vertices)
Precise definition of a periodic billiard path as one that returns to its initial position and direction after finitely many reflections
Clarification that the triangle’s sides are perfectly mirrored, frictionless, and elastic
Existence quantification: that there must be at least one choice of initial point and direction yielding a periodic orbit
refined_question: Let T be an arbitrary triangle in the Euclidean plane with its three sides acting as perfectly reflecting (mirrored), frictionless boundaries. Consider a point particle that moves in straight lines in the interior of T and undergoes specular reflection at the sides according to the law “angle of incidence equals angle of reflection,” and which is terminated if it ever reaches one of the triangle’s vertices. A billiard trajectory in T is called periodic if, after a finite number of reflections off the sides, the particle returns exactly to its initial position inside T with the same direction of motion. Does every triangle T admit at least one such periodic billiard trajectory?
justification: The title succinctly states the central question but omits the precise dynamical model (point particle, specular reflections, vertex extinction) and the formal definition of periodicity, hence a score of 7. The refined question incorporates these hidden assumptions and definitions exactly as given in the canonical source, without broadening or weakening the original formulation.

citations.label: A major open problem in this area concerns the existence of periodic billiards paths: does every triangle have a path that repeats its starting position and orientation after a finite number of reflections?
In this model, a light ray with a given initial position and orientation follows a polygonal chain reflecting by equal incidence and reflection angles and is extinguished upon reaching a vertex.
